experiences.description: This course covers the basic concepts of the theory of computation. To study computation thoroughly, we need models. Ideally, we would like simple models to solve our problems. This is what the theory of computation is about: computational models and their power, with an impressive array of applications. The practical models we study in this course include finite state machines, regular expressions, push-down automata, and context-free grammars. A crucial aspect is studying the limits of computations, which involves investigating all powerful models, such as Turing machines. Some problems are intractable, that is, it takes ages to solve them, others are provably impossible to solve even on an infinitely powerful computer. Computability theory sheds light on these issues of fundamental importance to anyone attempting to understand what computers can do for us.

At the core, software maintenance involves taking existing software artefacts, understanding them, and then modifying or extending the code and/or other work products associated with the software (such as requirements, design and test suites). Other aspects, such as migrating a system from one platform to another, reverse-engineering (i.e., extracting higher-level artefacts such as design from code), and inter-connecting existing systems for interoperability, are also part of this eld. It is estimated that 60-70% of the software development e ort in industry is maintenance and evolution. In this course, students will get practical experience in this field, working in a team, and addressing real-world issues of third-party systems.

The objective in this course is to share knowledge and technology on “software architectures”. A software architecture is an abstract representation of a software system,  filtering out what is traditionally considered detailed design- and implementationlevel issues (such as: algorithm, design patterns, data representation and coding) and highlighting such aspects as the overall system structure, inter-relationships and interaction among these the elements in the system structure, and other “run-time” or “off-line” properties of the system (such as reliability, performance, portability, inter-operability, etc.). Whereas the requirements of a system generally state the functionality and the expected behaviour of the deployed system, the architecture of the system  describes how the desired functions and qualities are to be (or have been) implemented. For a large and complex (software-intensive) system, its architecture is an essential means for controlling and evolving the system. Among many other uses of the architecture include: development team organisation, overall system test planning, training of new developers, release planning, defect analysis, system component reuse, size/cost/effort estimation, and vision sharing with various stakeholders. Just as there are patterns for the design of a system, there are patterns for the  architecture of the system. This helps in the selection of the entire, or parts of an, architecture from a set of choices; increasing reuse, cost reduction, and quality development.

experiences.experience_name: Bird Patroller and IT Volunteer at Fatal Light Awareness Program Canada
experiences.description:
I have a deep appreciation for the vital role birds play in our ecosystems, and I am passionate about raising awareness about the problem of bird collisions. One of my main interests lies in leveraging collision data for impactful solutions. Given FLAP’s extensive data collection over the years, I see tremendous potential in applying artificial intelligence to this dataset for predictive modeling and other innovative applications. Bird collisions remain underreported, and I believe that with better awareness and data collection, we can more accurately assess the problem and develop more effective prevention strategies.

As a FLAP patroller, I walk downtown routes during migration seasons to look for birds that have collided with windows. If a bird is stunned, I carefully contain it and send it to the Toronto Wildlife Centre for rehabilitation while documenting the collision. If a bird has been fatally injured, I collect and tag it. These specimens are valuable for education, raising awareness, and can also serve as food for other animals.

As an IT volunteer, I work closely with the Board of Directors to maintain and enhance the Global Bird Collision Mapper using ArcGIS tools. I help manage its database and contribute to adding new functionality to improve its usability and data accessibility. This role allows me to combine my technical skills and passion for bird conservation to support FLAP’s mission and create long-term solutions to reduce bird collisions.

experiences.experience_name: Undergraduate Summer Research Intern at Western University
experiences.description:
I worked with Dr. Mostafa Milani in Western's Database Lab to develop a deep learning model for medical imaging. My focus was creating a neural network to identify 16 lung conditions from 10,000 MRI chest scans. I researched and tested different tools and algorithms to improve accuracy while ensuring privacy, implementing solutions that balanced these priorities effectively.

I used TensorFlow Keras to build a convolutional neural network, applying K-fold cross-validation to validate results. I optimized the model using Optuna, refining its performance through careful tuning. To ensure the project’s continuity, I set up Anaconda environments and Jupyter Notebooks, onboarding a master’s student to continue the work smoothly.

The project also included a deep dive into differential privacy. I studied its effect on accuracy and applied these techniques to protect sensitive health data. Alongside this, I reviewed research on privacy in public health, designed a research proposal, and collected and analyzed data following ethical guidelines. My work helped explore how to protect health records without losing their value for research.
